en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Three Grades of Disciples, translated by the Ruyi Country layman Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
One thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus were assembled together to discourse on the sūtra.
The Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; may the God among Gods explain it for me, so that my doubts may be resolved!"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Ask whatever you wish."
"Tathāgata shall explain this for you.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"Among the upāsakas who study the Way, there are those of superior, middling, and inferior grades."
"I pray that the Buddha will explain this!
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "It is for the sake of future generations in later times that you have raised this question; the Tathāgata shall explain it to you."
"Listen attentively and receive this, internalizing it within your heart!
Ānanda replied,
"Yes, I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha said:
"The senior upāsakas and upāsikās uphold the five precepts without violating them even by so much as a hair’s breadth.
If they act as teachers to instruct and enlighten others, they cause all of them to resolve to attain the mind of a bodhisattva."
What is meant by the mind of a bodhisattva?
It is to regard the people of the ten directions as one would look upon an only child; to deliver beings into the Way and perform the practices of Mahāyāna;
to be fully endowed with instruction without harboring any expectations, and to seek no offerings such as clothing, food, precious gems, or wealth.
"Do not pursue minor paths; take the salvation of others as your fundamental purpose.
"What is meant by 'minor paths'?
The Buddha said:
"By entering the Great Dharma, one performs the practices of the Mahāyāna and seeks the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha."
This is but a minor path; it is not that of a bodhisattva.
The dharma of a bodhisattva consists in instructing all beings, causing them to enter the *prajñāpāramitā*, to understand *upāyakauśalya*, and to attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*).

You should know that such a person has long practiced these deeds; they were a person during the time of past Buddhas who made offerings to their teachers and preceptors no differently than to the Buddhas themselves.
A practitioner such as this is a supreme upāsaka or upāsikā.
"As for those of the middle grade—male and female lay followers—they also receive the five precepts and do not violate them even by so much as a hair’s breadth;
they were likewise people from the time of past Buddhas."

In practicing this Way, he did not encounter an enlightened teacher, nor did he hear the Prajñāpāramitā, nor was he proficient in upāyakauśalya; he practiced only a single pāramitā—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and concentration—and did not perceive wisdom within the sūtras and the Dharma.

Relying on previous merit, he was able to enter the human realm; possessing some residual consciousness from past lives, he attained the Dharma-gate of birth. He maintained the precepts in their entirety, regarding his teachers and elders as no different from the Buddha, and never violated the precepts.
A practitioner who acts in this manner is an Upāsaka or Upāsikā of the middle grade.
As for the Upāsakas and Upāsikās of the lower grade, although they have received the five precepts, they violate them all.
If one encounters an enlightened teacher or a wise person who understands the Dharma, one should immediately receive instruction on the essentials of the Dharma from them.
At that time, one should rejoice and repent for one's transgressions before them, redoubling one's diligence in observing the five precepts without any further backsliding.
Conceiving lustful desires, they no longer observe the Buddha’s precepts.
Becoming arrogant, they instead harbor hatred toward their enlightened teachers and virtuous companions, slandering them by speaking of their faults:
"I have now seen that my enlightened teacher’s precepts are profound and his wisdom deep; I shall protect him through skillful means!"
Not realizing that this teacher merely consumes their offerings, they instead place faith in and accept his words, failing to cultivate themselves in the sutras and the precepts.
Such upāsakas and upāsikās are of the same lineage as those who carry the dead; one ought not to associate with them, nor sit or rise together with them.

They ruin the good intentions and practices of others, seeking to convert the people so that they might receive their teachings and precepts; they hope for offerings, desiring to obtain money, grain, and silk to provide for their wives and children.

Relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, though their hearts do not think of the beings within the five realms of existence in the ten directions whom they wish to deliver and liberate, they instead form conceptualizations regarding those who receive [their gifts] and do not speak of the wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
This constitutes a failure to cultivate the Buddha’s true and correct Dharma, as one says to those who receive the scriptures:
"One should avoid the causal conditions of worldly people, yet drink a small amount of alcohol."
The Buddha has food of a hundred flavors, yet he does not prohibit people from drinking wine.

As for those in a household who do not uphold the precepts—whether they be servants, guests, slaves, or laborers—one may request others to slaughter living beings on their behalf; one must simply refrain from raising one's own hand to commit the act.
“Those who are not disciples of the Buddha further limit the merit of the Buddha.
[The interlocutor asked: “In what way do they limit the merit of the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"Having already begun to teach and bestow [the Dharma] upon the people, I do not wish for the fourfold assembly to hear of it.
Ānanda knelt down and asked the Buddha,
"Why do you not wish for the fourfold assembly to hear of it?"
"These upāsakas and upāsikās are of dull minds and lack understanding; they consider themselves wise, yet in truth they do not comprehend the profound and essential wisdom within the sūtras."

Not feeling shame for one's own ignorance, they instead create obstacles for those who are newly learned and virtuous, not wishing to let them see clear understanding or encounter excellent teachers. Why is this?
Because they desire exclusive offerings for themselves, they conversely obscure and block the Great Way.

Although these upāsakas and upāsikās lead others across [to liberation], they do not perceive the prajñāpāramitā and do not understand *upāyakauśalya*. Thus, they are blind and deluded, practicing only the minor paths;
they may teach others to perform meritorious deeds, yet they lack the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and their giving does not reach all.
"Please set this aside; the Way and its Law do not employ it.

Then the messengers who are the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings and the deities who protect the Buddha-way shall record each instance one by one, gradually distancing themselves [from the offender], and command the Lords of Life to calculate and accumulate their transgressions, itemizing their names and reporting them to the Supreme Deity.
Before their life span is exhausted, malevolent spirits are suddenly dispatched; because they have transgressed the precepts, their remaining life is snatched away.

They naturally fall into the *niraya* hells, where they must undergo the punishments of eighteen hells until the heavens and earth are consumed by fire before they emerge. Thereafter, they may fall among the birds and beasts, or enter the human realm.
"If one is in the human realm, one will remain in ignorance and fail to see the birth of the Dharma-family.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

"The Way requires frequent assemblies for discussion and exposition; the principles of the Dharma must not be obstructed. For the foolish, the Way should lead to the severing of dharmas and the extinguishing of the offenses against the Buddha's teachings.
When the disciples heard the Buddha preach this sutra, there was none who did not tremble with awe; they all rectified their minds to receive the instruction and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Three Grades of Disciples.
